Chapter Eight: The Rise of Administrative Power and the Threat to Freedom
As towns turned into bustling cities, and the nation stretched from one coast to the other, government naturally grew more complicated. What started out as just a few local officials and some simple rules slowly transformed into this sprawling web of agencies, regulations, and bureaucracy. For a lot of folks, that seemed like progress—a way to handle the growing pains of a changing society.
But not everyone saw it that way. The rise of administrative power brought a new set of worries. Those old habits of self-government—things like town meetings and local associations—started to slip away. Suddenly, decisions were made by officials you’d never meet, following rules hardly anyone could really understand. Imagine a shopkeeper who once helped shape the future of his town, now just trying to untangle endless red tape. Or a teacher, full of new ideas, stuck in a maze of regulations.
Most people don’t even notice how power shifts over time. It’s gradual—responsibilities quietly passed to experts and specialists. Usually, it’s with good intentions: to keep things fair, protect the vulnerable, or keep order. But gradually, that everyday sense of agency—the feeling that you can help steer your own community—starts to fade.
Here’s something to pay attention to: even though bureaucracy can make life more organized, it can also hide some real dangers. When folks feel powerless, they start to tune out. They disconnect from their community. And without that habit of participation—so crucial for democracy—something important begins to wither. Instead, people start thinking, “Nothing I do can really change anything.”
Some folks respond by turning inward, focusing on their own lives and personal success. Others get frustrated, demanding reform or even revolution. That tension—between withdrawal and protest—shapes our politics. It’s what drives the cycles of hope, disappointment, and sometimes even anger that we see in the country.
But here’s the real takeaway: government isn’t the enemy. It’s just a reminder that freedom needs watchfulness. The machinery of administration should work for us—not the other way around. If we want to keep our liberty, we have to stay involved. We have to insist on transparency, on accountability, and on real participation. That’s how a society protects its freedom, no matter how complex things get.
